newsitem.title: INDIA: GOLD-Demand revival seen in Indian subcontinent.
newsitem.headline: GOLD-Demand revival seen in Indian subcontinent.

text.p: India's appetite for gold is expected to pick up with the end of the seasonal June-July lean period, sparking a rise in imports, dealers said on Monday.
They said demand from India, the world's largest importer of gold, would be firm for at least four months from August onwards because of approaching Hindu festivals.
"This will lead to good demand for gold in Dubai," said Bombay Bullion Association president Makhan Lal Damani.
Dealers in Karachi, Pakistan's main commercial city, said last week's fall in domestic gold prices could trigger demand for gold jewellery in the next few days.
Dealers in the Gulf trading city of Dubai, the re-export market that feeds demand in the Indian subcontinent, said they expected domestic retail sales to rise in August.
"Indian rural demand will pick up from August," Damani said. It normally lies dormant in June and July with the onset of the four-month monsoon, ending in September.
"The monsoon has generally been good across the country, except in a few pockets. Farmers will come to the market to buy gold with the first earnings from the winter harvest," said Damani.

Gold prices on the Bombay bullion market, however, fell 40 rupees per 10 grams to 4,525 rupees in the week to Monday following a weak world trend. Bombay dealers said they were awaiting the start of festival buying of gold in August, which traditionally peaks at the time of Diwali, the festival of lights, towards the end of October.
"I am expecting gold prices to fluctuate with world prices in the coming days but to firm later," said leading bullion dealer Babubhai Jain.
Dealers in Karachi said they expected gold prices to remain stable on a rise in demand.
"Demand for gold jewellery will rise as gold prices have fallen sharply," dealer Sajid Siddiqi said, adding the rise in demand will give stability to prices.

In Dubai, dealers said stable gold prices could boost demand from the Indian subcontinent. But key Indian import demand remained largely blunted because of the monsoons and market nerves over the possibility of more gold reserve selling by central banks.
"Most Indian importers are holding off wanting to confirm the direction in the market, to see if it has reached a bottom," said another trader.
